source.title_on_document: Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort

supplement.where: Supplementary Information, PDF pp. 11-41 (SI pages 1-31; SI page k = PDF page 10+k)
supplement.holds: Arm means with SEs and standardized effects (d) with SEs for writing quality by phase (Tables S6, S7, S12 for Study 2; S19, S20 for Study 3; S28, S29, S34, S35 for Study 4), beta regressions for interview likelihood (S15, S25, S38), randomization and balance tables with arm ns (S5, S18, S27), missingness and attrition (S4, S17, S26), rating prompts (S1).

paper_design_summary: Three preregistered online experiments with Prolific participants (Studies 2-4) and one Gallup attitude survey (Study 1). After a pretest and a lesson on five professional-writing principles, participants were randomly assigned to practice rewriting a cover letter with an AI rewriting tool, without it, with no practice, with professional editor feedback, with Google Search, or by viewing an AI-rewritten example; all then rewrote a new cover letter without AI (and again one day later in Studies 2 and 4). The scored output is cover-letter writing quality, rated by GPT-4o as the mean adherence to the five principles (0-10), plus a lay-rater pairwise measure of the likelihood of a hypothetical interview; no creativity, novelty, or diversity outcome is scored.

outcomes.name: Test-phase writing quality (no AI)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4o rates each letter 0-10 on each of the five writing principles, separately; outcome is the unweighted mean (preregistered main DV). ANCOVA controlling for pretest and baseline covariates. Robustness: Claude ratings, no controls, excluding admitted cheaters, follow-up subsample, each principle separately (all in Table S7). eligibility.reason: Studies 2-4 randomly assign Prolific participants (2,238, 2,997, 2,003) to practice with a generative-AI rewriting tool versus no AI, no practice, editor feedback, or Google Search, so criteria 1 and 2 are met. The task is rewriting a cover letter to five professional-writing principles (concision, easy reading, navigation, formatting, easy responding), and the outcome is GPT-4o-rated adherence to those principles plus a lay-rater interview-likelihood choice. Neither is creativity, novelty, ideation, or diversity across people, so criterion 3 fails and the task falls outside the codebook's creative or ideation scope. The paper would fit the learning section (after-AI skill), not the creativity section.

one_line_finding: Participants who practiced cover-letter writing with an AI rewriting tool later wrote better letters without AI than those who practiced alone (d = .38, Table S7; d = .41 one day later, Table S12), than those who got professional editor feedback (d = .20) or used Google Search (d = .46, Table S20), and viewing an AI example matched practicing with AI (d = .04, Table S29); the outcome is writing quality, not creativity.
open_questions: Is cover-letter quality judged on professional-writing principles inside the creativity scope? Screener A says no (outcome is clarity and format adherence, not creativity, novelty, or diversity); the candidate record also flags it as writing quality, not creativity.

Exact counts analyzed for the writing-quality regressions are not printed: Fig. S3 and Fig. S12 state the full Ns (2,238; 2,003) despite 3.31 and 5.64 percent missing text; Study 3's test count after 14 percent attrition is not printed (interview model N = 2,575).
Table S15 (Study 2) uses Study 4 arm labels ('See AI example') and its without-controls column is identical to Table S38 (Study 4: N = 1934, phi = 16.17), which suggests a copy error in the SI.
notes: Study 1 N disagrees between main text (2,637, p. 3) and SI (2,472, PDF p. 14). Study 4 test d for Practice w/ AI vs w/o AI is .34 in the main text (p. 6) but .32 in Table S29. Study 3 SI d values carry a negative sign for 'AI vs. X' even though AI means are higher (Tables S19, S20); main text reports them as positive. Fig. 7 caption on p. 6 says 'Study 4 participants' but describes Study 3. Study 3 return interval: 'the following day' (p. 5) vs 'two days after the initial intake section' (SI D1, PDF p. 24). Main text says 49 editors (p. 5); SI D2 says 44 editors who edited 1,227 letters (PDF p. 25). Each study also ran a separate forecaster sample (N = 150 each for Studies 2 and 3) on predictions and willingness to pay; these have no scored output and are not coded as studies. Effort outcomes (time, keystrokes, self-reported effort) and self-reported learning are not scored on the output and are omitted.
